metadata.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI will match Anthropic’s new AI safety commitment, Musk says ‘Dario is right’

sources.news_title: Amodei said faster model development could raise catastrophic risks, and Altman and Musk backed calls for companies to voluntarily slow the frontier.
sources.text:
Le patron d'Anthropic appelle à ralentir le développement de l'intelligence artificielle
Le patron d'Anthropic, Dario Amodei, a appelé samedi à ralentir la vitesse de développement de l'intelligence artificielle (IA), un message auquel se sont rapidement rallié Elon Musk et Sam Altman (OpenAI).
Publié le : Modifié le :
Les patrons américains de l'Intelligence artificielle disent vouloir mettre le pied sur le frein concernant le développement de l'intelligence artificielle. Le patron d’Anthropic, le concepteur de Claude, a appelé à ralentir le développement de l’IA pour avoir le temps de prévenir les risques de débordement en parallèle. Quelques heures plus tard, Elon Musk, patron de xAI, a lâché sur son propre réseau social X que « Dario Amodei avait raison ». Et dans la foulée, Sam Altman, patron d’OpenAI a opiné du chef.
Un ralliement rare pour ces concurrents qui confirme l'inquiétude qui regne quant aux manquements de sécurité des technologies d'intelligence artificielle. Par exemple, en juin, des modèles d’OpenAI étaient sortis spontanément de leur milieu de tests pour attaquer une autre plateforme d’IA.
Depuis, plusieurs autres événements ayant vu des IA d'OpenAI et Anthropic se rendre sur internet à l'insu de leurs superviseurs ont été rapportés par les deux entreprises. À chaque fois, ils impliquaient des agents IA, c'est-à-dire un programme spécifique bâti sur un modèle et doté de ses propres connaissances et de ses propres objectifs.
Les agissements et les méthodes de ces agents ont d'autant plus inquiété qu'ils ont montré une propension à se coordonner, à établir une hiérarchie entre eux, à tricher et à effacer les traces de leurs méfaits.
« Prendre le contrôle de l'intégralité d'internet »
Il y a aussi la peur que l’IA prenne le contrôle d’internet. Vu l'accélération actuelle du développement de l'IA, « je redoute que d'ici 6 à 12 mois, un groupe (d'agents) soit capable de prendre le contrôle de l'intégralité d'internet », a prévenu Dario Amodei, ce qui « pourrait entraîner des centaines de milliards de dollars de dégâts ».
Pourtant, après avoir identifié les dérapages de leurs modèles, OpenAI et Anthropic avaient chacun suspendu ou freiné le travail sur leurs nouvelles IA durant quelques jours, avant de le reprendre au même rythme. Mardi, Jacob Coxon, salarié démissionnaire d'Anthropic et ancien d'OpenAI, avait dénoncé l'inertie des deux concurrents. « Aucune des deux entreprises n'agit de manière responsable. Elles foncent tout droit vers une superintelligence capable de s'améliorer elle-même et jouent avec nos vies », a-t-il écrit sur le réseau social X.
Outre son appel, Dario Amodei formule plusieurs propositions, en premier lieu, l'intégration par les fleurons de l'IA d'observateurs indépendants. S'il la recommande à toute l'industrie, le dirigeant s'engage à la mettre en place unilatéralement chez Anthropic. Samedi, Sam Altman a promis d'en faire de même chez OpenAI.
Dario Amodei prône aussi la collaboration entre les entreprises les plus avancées pour définir des normes de sécurité communes. Il se dit aussi favorable à une forme de coordination politique entre toutes les grandes nations de l'IA.

The tech billionaires Elon Musk and Sam Altman have backed a call from the head of Anthropic for the artificial intelligence industry to “slow down” to give safety measures time to catch up.
In an essay titled ‘We Must Pace the Frontier‘, Dario Amodei said he is concerned that since this summer AI has been “advancing drastically faster”.
Given the rate of AI development, Amodei is worried that within six to 12 months it could be capable of leading a swarm that could take over the entire internet.
The entrepreneur, whose company is behind the AI assistant Claude and who was previously a senior figure at Altman’s company OpenAI, shared a three-part plan for building the technology at a “balanced rate”.
“I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong,” Amodei said.
The essay has been supported by other industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of xAI whose X site carries the AI chatbot Grok, and Sam Altman, whose OpenAI makes ChatGPT.
Responding to Amodei’s essay on X, Musk wrote: “Dario is right.”
Altman wrote on the social media site: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.
“Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”
Amodei offered a plan to increase checks on the industry, proposing that AI companies should give access to third-party evaluators who would verify safety practices and report incidents.
“Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now,” he said.
The other steps would require co-ordination among the broad industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
Amodei said AI is developing quickly, adding that companies within the industry “can and should voluntarily work together to set standards”.
Anthropic previously said it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.
In July, OpenAI shook the industry after saying its AI system hacked into another company on its own in an “unprecedented cyber incident.”

Sam Altman and Elon Musk back calls to ‘slow down’ AI development over safety concerns
‘We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,’ says Dario Amodei
Leading tech figures Sam Altman and Elon Musk have aligned themselves with a call from the head of Anthropic for the artificial intelligence (AI) sector to "slow down" and allow safety measures to keep pace.
In an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”, Dario Amodei warned that the development of AI has been "advancing drastically faster" since the summer.
He expressed concern that, at current rates of progress, AI could be equipped within six to 12 months to command a swarm capable of taking over the internet.
The entrepreneur, whose company developed the Claude AI assistant, proposed a three-stage roadmap designed to foster innovation at a "balanced rate".
"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Mr Amodei said.
Prominent industry voices have rallied behind the essay, including Mr Musk and Mr Altman.
Replying to Mr Amodei’s essay on X, Mr Musk wrote: "Dario is right."
OpenAI chief executive Mr Altman wrote on the platform: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.
"Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon."
Mr Amodei’s proposals include granting external evaluators access to monitor corporate safety mechanisms and log potential risks.
"Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now," he said.
Subsequent stages would demand international co-ordination across the wider industry and among governments globally, including authoritarian states.
Highlighting how rapidly the technology is evolving, Mr Amodei said tech firms "can and should voluntarily work together to set standards".
Anthropic has previously disclosed that it stopped bad actors using its systems for harmful ends, such as cyber attacks, surveillance, and work that could assist in creating biological weapons.
Worry over potential harm from AI deepened this week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, stating that the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
The warnings follow an admission in July by OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, that its system had independently breached another company in an "unprecedented cyber incident."
Elsewhere, Altman said in a Fortune interview published Saturday, that OpenAI will not go public in 2026 citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence.
"I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," Altman told Fortune.
When asked whether 2026 is off the table in favour of 2027, Altman said, "I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together."
